https://www.nottinghampost.com/news/loca.text: Five residents cram into a tiny room in a bungalow in Mansfield . As one of them starts telling her story, she immediately starts crying. “I’m afraid to go outside, to walk with the dogs,” she sobs. “My grandson is nine months old. I’m afraid to take him out as well.” Her name is Malgorzata Pead and, for the last few years, she claims she has suffered threats, harassment and abuse from a neighbour. Those in the room allege the same. They say they have come to the Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS) because “no one else wants to help”. But the neighbour in question says the people accusing her do the same thing back. All parties involved want action to resolve the dispute, but so far, nothing has changed. The street where they live is a cul-de-sac of council homes, where rows of bungalows face each other. Andrzej Zyla and his partner Aneta, who are Polish like Ms Pead, moved here in November 2024. They say that the abuse started on the day they moved in, and within a week, they’d contacted the council about it. Within a month, they’d contacted the police . “She spits at people,” says Andrzej. “She calls us names, she’s very aggressive, she parks her car in front of our car to block us in.” But when the Local Democracy Reporting Service spoke to the neighbour, she said that she had lived in the area for more than a year by the time Mr Zyla moved in – and that nobody had had a problem with her before. She said: “I’ve tried to move out. I’m being antagonised, and I don’t know how to handle it. I’ve asked them to leave me alone. Some weeks I can’t do it. I’ve had enough. It’s not fair.” Mr Zyla and the other residents say they “completely deny” the woman’s allegations and say “we have never threatened, intimidated or harassed her.” The LDRS has seen video footage and photographs which appear to show the neighbour spitting towards Mr Zyla’s home, swearing at them and calling them “stupid” in Polish and making insulting comments about Mr Zyla’s weight. The neighbour says that she has only reacted to situations instigated by others. In one piece of video footage, the neighbour is heard telling a postman not to leave a parcel for Mr Zyla on her property because she fears being accused of stealing it. Aneta says she has been to the GP because of the stress from the row. “It’s given me mental health issues,” she says through a translator. “I’m on tablets. I have to go out at 5am for work, and I’m afraid of what’s going to happen.” Andrzej says he has to pick his partner up from work every day because they “don’t know what she is going to do next”. The pair have sent their video and photographic evidence to the council and the police on a USB stick. Most of the video was captured by CCTV cameras that Mr Zyla & Aneta had installed on their house. But after doing this, the couple received a letter themselves accusing them of anti-social behaviour, including “CCTV cameras that are invading privacy of the neighbours and community” and “intimidation and harassment of your neighbour”. Other accusations included “goading of your neighbour into a reaction which you are then filming”, “placing your dustbins in the way of vehicles preventing access/exit” and “unnecessary calls to the local police”. The council threatened to repossess the property or, as new residents, extend their six-month probation period if the behaviour did not stop. In March 2026, a Community Protection Warning was issued under the Anti-Social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014 – but not to Mr Zyla and Agneta. It states that their neighbour “shall not directly or indirectly cause harassment, alarm or distress” to nearby residents or visitors. It also bans her from contacting directly or indirectly Mr Zyla, Aneta or Ms Pead. The group say the situation is not being taken seriously enough by the authorities. More recently, the group has been involved in meetings with the council and the police, which Mr Zyla said he initially felt were productive and promising. He hoped that the neighbour would be issued with an escalated anti-social behaviour warning, but was told that “no breaches have been recorded” of the CPW. He was also told, as the main complainant, that other affected residents’ witness statements would not be taken into account in the authorities’ decision on how to proceed. The police told the couple to be “mindful of their own responses” to the neighbour and advised “that the nature of a response to perceived issues can unintentionally escalate matters or create further conflict.” Notes from their last meeting say that the reported incidents “do not meet the threshold for a crime”. Mr Zyla and Aneta have applied to move home and have now been allocated a caseworker to support them through the process. “We need help,” says Mr Zyla. “We want to live a normal life. Not a scared one.” Cllr Anne Callaghan, Mansfield District Council’s Portfolio Holder for Housing, said: “We cannot comment on individual cases, but we take all reports of antisocial behaviour very seriously. As a responsible landlord, we have thoroughly looked into the issues raised and followed our legal duties. “We know antisocial behaviour can make people feel unsafe and upset, and we understand the impact it has on residents and the wider community. “We work closely with the police and base our actions on evidence to make sure they are fair and appropriate towards everyone and meet legal thresholds. We ask anyone affected to keep reporting incidents, as this helps us build the evidence needed to take further action.” Inspector Katie Eustace of Nottinghamshire Police, said: “We have received a number of reports relating to an ongoing neighbour dispute and we are working with council partners to address issues raised by both sides. “Both parties have raised issues, including reported incidents of antisocial behaviour, harassment and criminal damage. Lines of inquiry have been carried out in relation to incidents reported to us, including checking CCTV footage, but no evidence was found of any offences being committed.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: Novaya Gazeta editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov talks to the media outside the newspaper’s Moscow office in October 2021. Photograph: Alexander Zemlianichenko/AP View image in fullscreen Novaya Gazeta editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov talks to the media outside the newspaper’s Moscow office in October 2021. Photograph: Alexander Zemlianichenko/AP Opinion Russia Moscow has shuttered Novaya Gazeta – we told the truth and we paid the price Elena Kostyuchenko Russia’s best-known independent newspaper was my home for 17 years. It’s being shut down, but the spirit of its journalism will live on Sat 7 Nov 2026 03.00 EST Last modified on Sat 7 Nov 2026 03.41 EST Share N ovaya Gazeta – Russia’s most prominent independent newspaper – is being shut down . On 29 October, two things became known: Novaya was being evicted from its newsroom, and banks would stop processing readers’ donations to Novaya (its only legal income). Insiders spoke of the risk of Novaya being declared an extremist organisation – then any employee could be jailed: a journalist, an editor, an accountant, a cleaner. Closing was safer. Novaya Gazeta is a second family to me and to many journalists now scattered around the Earth. For me it is my first family, too – my adopted sister also worked at Novaya, and it’s funny how alike we turned out. I bought Novaya for the first time when I was 14. I opened it to an article by Anna Politkovskaya about the “cleansing” of the Chechen village of Mesker-Yurt by Russian soldiers. Thirty-six people were killed; one man was crucified . None of it made sense to me. I considered myself well informed; like everyone around me, I knew exactly what was happening in Chechnya. Our soldiers were heroically protecting civilians from terrorists. The more I read, the more I realised that I knew nothing about my own country. I was angry at Novaya. It took away the truth I shared with everyone else. I couldn’t ignore it – the words would not be forgotten. Later, I understood that this is exactly what journalism should be: it should drag you back to reality, even when you don’t want to go. A few years later, I was working at the paper. I came to Novaya at 17 with no connections, not knowing how to turn on a computer – and I stayed for 17 years. Novaya rarely hired established journalists – it took very young kids and nurtured them. The youngest people in the newsroom were 15, the oldest close to 80. It was one big, intergenerational school. Today, people from Novaya work at almost every independent Russian outlet. The paper wrote about the most important things in a way that turned the words themselves into events: Beslan, the purge of gay men in Chechnya, Malaysia Airlines flight MH17, corruption, the wars in Chechnya, Georgia, Syria and Ukraine, torture, organised crime, the environment, terrorism – and the people living very different lives across our vast country. In 1993, just a few months after Novaya Gazeta was established, Boris Yeltsin, then the president, dissolved the Supreme Soviet, our country’s parliament. The army shelled the White House in Moscow using tanks. Officially, 158 people died; unofficial estimates are higher. Novaya’s special issue carried reports from the White House, from the streets and hospitals under the headline: “As long as we divide even the dead into our own and our enemies, the war will go on.” That was the paper’s true motto. View image in fullscreen Dmitry Muratov is hugged by colleagues at the paper after being awarded a Nobel peace prize in 2021. Photograph: Alexander Zemlianichenko/AP Dmitry Muratov, one of Novaya Gazeta’s founders and editors-in-chief, liked to say: “The work only begins once the text is published.” When I wrote about a former orphanage kid wrongly convicted of murder, Novaya Gazeta found him a lawyer, and for several years we went to the hearings until he was acquitted. Novaya’s investigations became the basis of criminal cases, lives were saved (Anna Politkovskaya organised the evacuation of 89 elderly people abandoned in a nursing home in Grozny). In the paper’s 33 years, six of its people were killed: Igor Domnikov, Yuri Shchekochikhin , Politkovskaya, Stanislav Markelov , Anastasia Baburova, Natalia Estemirova . In most cases, those who ordered the killings were never found or punished. Many Novaya journalists received threats. Many were beaten. Someone splashed a chemical in Muratov’s face; his eyes were saved. When Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine began in February 2022, Novaya Gazeta came out in Russian and Ukrainian with a clear message on the front page: “We refuse to see the Ukrainian people as our enemies.” A month later, Novaya had to suspend publication; the authorities took away its licence and printing the paper became impossible. The website was blocked. Social networks were blocked too, for the whole country. In April of this year, the newsroom was searched and equipment was seized; at the same time, the investigative journalist Oleg Roldugin was arrested, and he is now awaiting trial. On 4 September, the Ministry of Justice declared Novaya a “foreign agent” – along with 106 of its contributors. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Matters of Opinion Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more after newsletter promotion I Love Russia by Elena Kostyuchenko review – reportage at its best Read more Many now say it was a miracle that Novaya Gazeta kept working inside Russia for four and a half years of war, when almost all independent media had moved their newsrooms abroad. This miracle was made possible by the daily choices of people I love and of those I have not met yet. They were afraid to come to the newsroom – but they came every single day. They went to the occupied territories, investigated, documented the repression, talked to people as people, without simplifying, generalising, or looking away. Many kept prison bags in their hallways – clothes and medicine packed in case of arrest. Everyone learned their lawyer’s number by heart. Everyone gave their neighbours a set of keys so – if anything happened – someone would water the plants and feed the cats. For my colleagues, I feel gratitude and love, fear, endless admiration and endless pain. For the Russian state that set out to kill Novaya Gazeta and has now killed it, I feel nothing. The drive to know the truth ( even when it hurts terribly ) is built into every human heart, written into our biology; it is a condition of our survival. That is why Novaya will be eternal, even when every one of us is gone. Elena Kostyuchenko is a Russian journalist and the author of I Love Russia: Reporting from a Lost Country Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
